power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Autistic people experience high rates of mental health conditions and barriers to accessing supports.
Digital mental health interventions (DMHIs) may be one way to improve access, but their applicability is unclear.
We reviewed DMHIs that focus on mental health outcomes in autistic people, examining their scope, adaptation, community involvement and evidence of effectiveness.
Five databases were searched in 08/2024 and 04/2026.
Eligible studies evaluated a DMHI and reported pre-post mental health outcomes in autistic people.
Findings were synthesised narratively using SWiM guidelines.
Thirty-three studies reported on 1,258 autistic participants across fifteen studies were randomised controlled trials and 17 uncontrolled designs.
Although anxiety was the primary focus of DMHIs, effects of DMHIs on depression, specific phobia, obsessive-compulsive disorder and trauma were also explored.
Comparative findings for anxiety were mixed, and the predominantly small and uncontrolled evidence base could not establish efficacy.
Most interventions were CBT-based, community involvement in study or DMHI design was very limited.
DMHIs could be a promising option to support the mental health of autistic people, but research is in preliminary stages.
Future studies should focus on co-producing DMHIs and embedding these into adequately powered controlled studies that are inclusive for a broader range of participants.
Why did we do this study?
Autistic people are more likely to experience mental health difficulties, but many find it hard to access support that is affordable, available, and suited to their needs.
Digital approaches, such as therapy delivered through video calls, websites, apps, or online programs, could help make support more accessible.
However, it is important to know whether these approaches work for autistic people, and for whom.
We looked for all of the research on digital approaches to supporting mental health of Autistic people.

We found 33 published studies and examined the types of support offered, whether the support actually improved mental health, who took part in the studies, and how autistic people were involved in the research.
What did we find?
We found that most of the digital supports have focussed on anxiety and used cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT).
The findings were mixed.
Some studies found that digital interventions helped reduce anxiety, while others found little or no benefit.
There may be some promising results for depression, but there were not enough high-quality studies to draw firm conclusions.
Many studies were small or lacked a comparison group, making it difficult to know how much improvement was due to the intervention itself.
We also found important gaps in the research.
Few studies included autistic people with intellectual disability, and most were conducted in Western countries.
Autistic people were rarely involved in designing the interventions or shaping the research.
Many studies also did not explain whether the tools they used to measure mental health were appropriate for autistic people.
What should we do next?
Overall, digital mental health supports show promise, but there is not yet enough evidence to know which approaches work best, for whom, and under what circumstances.
Making a program available online does not automatically make it accessible or useful.
Future research should work in partnership with autistic people, include a wider range of participants, compare different approaches fairly, and report both benefits and potential harms.
This will help autistic people, families, clinicians, and services make better-informed decisions about digital mental health support.
Autistic people have an elevated likelihood of experiencing mental health disorders.

Metaanalytic studies suggest that both current and lifetime rates of anxiety disorder and depression are higher in autistic compared to non-autistic populations (Hollocks et al., 2019; Lai et al., 2019; Polanczyk et al., 2015; Steel et al., 2014), with estimates suggesting a two to four times increased risk across the lifetime (Hudson et al., 2019; Nimmo-Smith et al., 2020).

text.text: Digital mental health interventions (DMHIs) are one approach to addressing barriers to accessing mental health supports.
DMHIs deliver information, support and/or psychological therapy through technological or digital platforms, with or without therapist support.
They include computerassisted therapy, apps, wearable devices, virtual reality therapy and interactive videos or DVDs.

They have been described as having "enormous potential" as a scalable solution for narrowing the service provision gap (Gan et al., 2021, pg. 764079) due to their affordability, efficiency, anonymity and accessibility.

text.text: DMHIs have been widely researched in non-autistic people; a meta-analysis of 47 randomised controlled trials (RCTs) with 4,958 participants showed a large effect size (g = 0.80) for DMHIs for anxiety (Pauley et al., 2023) and a medium effect size (g = 0.52; 83 studies, 15,530 participants) for depression (Moshe et al., 2021).

text.text: However, given the increasing volume of evidence that the presentation and mechanisms of mental health conditions may differ in autistic people (Hinze et al., 2024; Hwang et al., 2020; South & Rodgers, 2017), it cannot be assumed that approaches that work for non-autistic people will work in autistic people.

text.text: Indeed, large observational cohort studies from England show that primary care psychological therapy services were significantly less effective for treating depression and anxiety in autistic adults than adults without identified autism (El Baou et al., 2023).

text.text: Therefore, whilst there is a large body of research evaluating DMHIs in the general population, it is important to evaluate the current research on DMHIs specifically in autistic people.
Establishing whether DMHIs are suitable for autistic people requires consideration beyond their effects on mental health outcomes.
DMHIs may overcome some barriers associated with conventional service delivery, but digital delivery alone does not ensure accessibility or suitability for all autistic people.

When evaluating evidence for DMHIs for autistic people, it is important to establish who is represented within the evidence base and who has been excluded (see <anonymised for review>), as the heterogeneity of autistic profiles means that DMHIs may not be equally acceptable, feasible or effective in increasing autistic people's access to mental health support.

text.text: Additionally, it is important to consider how relevant the DMHI is to autistic people, and whether autistic people were involved in the design of the study or the DMHI itself.
Autistic adults and psychologists have identified autistic-informed, person-centred support as a core principle of neurodiversity-affirming psychology practice (Flower et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Autistic adults and psychologists have identified autistic-informed, person-centred support as a core principle of neurodiversity-affirming psychology practice <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Flower et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, the emerging evidence that mental health conditions may present differently in autistic people raises questions about whether outcome measures developed for non-autistic populations adequately measure intervention effects in autistic participants (Cassidy et al., 2018), so any evaluation of evidence of DMHIs in autistic people must carefully consider the outcome measures used.

text.text: Previous reviews have examined digital interventions, programs and supports focused on social skills, communication, language or other developmental outcomes (e.g. Wang et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2026).

text.text: However, to the authors' knowledge, no systematic review has specifically examined DMHIs for autistic people.
The present review therefore aimed to characterise the scope, quality and applicability of the existing evidence on DMHIs for autistic people by addressing the following research questions: 1.
What are the characteristics of studies evaluating DMHIs for autistic people, and who has been represented in this research?
What DMHIs have been evaluated for autistic people, how have they been delivered and adapted for autistic people?

Which mental health conditions and outcomes have DMHIs focused on, what evidence is there regarding their effectiveness and how appropriate are the measures used to assess these outcomes for autistic people?
What is the methodological and reporting quality of the existing evidence, and to what extent have autistic people been involved in the design and conduct of this research?
The protocol for this systematic review was registered online with PROSPERO, an international register for systematic reviews with health-related outcomes (Registration number: <anonymised>).
text.formatted: The protocol for this systematic review was registered online with PROSPERO, an international register for systematic reviews with health-related outcomes (Registration number: <anonymised>).

text.text: Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) standards were followed for all stages of this systematic review.

Studies were eligible if they (a) evaluated a digitally delivered psychological support, program or intervention that is (b) designed to target a mental health condition either directly or through a parent/caregiver, and they reported a (c) pre-post mental health outcome using interview, questionnaire or clinical rating data for (d) autistic people.

Studies were excluded if (a) the digital component related only to pharmaceutical prescribing, (b) the study only reported on assessment or treatment adherence; if the DMHI (c) targeted parent/carer rather than autistic mental health or (d) targeted outcomes other than mental health; (e) if the study reported acceptability or experience without pre-post mental health outcomes; or (f) did not report original data.
No restrictions were placed on participant age, publication language or date.
Grey and non-peer-reviewed literature identified through the search was eligible to reduce potential publication bias (Johnson, 2021).
text.formatted: Grey and non-peer-reviewed literature identified through the search was eligible to reduce potential publication bias <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Johnson, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The Cochrane Library and PROSPERO database were searched to confirm that no other systematic reviews of the current study topic existed or were registered as being in progress.
Five electronic databases (MEDLINE, PubMed, PsycINFO, Scopus, Proquest) were searched in August 2024 and updated on 27 April 2026 with no date restrictions.

The search terms (applied to title, abstract and keyword searches) were related to three topics, which were combined with the Boolean operator AND: autism (autis* OR asperger* OR asd OR pdd OR pervasive developmental disorder), mental health (Wellbeing OR Mental Health OR Mental Disorder* OR Anxi* OR Depressi* OR Dysthymic Disorder OR Mood Disorders OR Panic* OR Phobi* OR Obsessive-compulsive disorder OR Post-Traumatic OR Eating Disorders OR Psychotic Disorders OR Schizophrenia OR Bipolar) AND digital delivery (Digital OR online OR self-paced OR self-help OR self-directed OR selfinstruction OR self-guided OR mHealth OR eHealth OR web-based OR internet-based OR mobile phone OR text message OR SMS OR artificial intelligence OR telehealth OR remote OR App OR Mobile Applications OR Telemedicine OR Web Browser OR Virtual Reality Exposure Therapy OR Video Games OR Phone* OR Computer OR tele-health OR teletherapy OR telemedicine).
Combined the original and update searches identified 4,307 records, which were imported into Covidence.
Following removal of 1,311 duplicates, titles and abstracts were independently screened by two reviewers, with 98.3% agreement.
Fifty-six reports underwent full-text screening by both reviewers, with 92.9% agreement.
Disagreements at both stages were resolved by discussion and consensus until 100% agreement was reached.

Data extracted included study and sample characteristics, DMHI characteristics, mental health targets and outcomes, measurement time points, comparison or control conditions, effect estimates and associated statistics, engagement metrics, and whether outcomes were designated primary or secondary.
Data from 50% of included reports were independently extracted by two reviewers, with disagreements resolved through discussion, resulting in 100% agreement.
The remaining reports were extracted by one reviewer.
Given the heterogeneity in DMHI characteristics, study designs, comparators, outcome measures, and statistical reporting, a meta-analysis was not considered appropriate.
Findings were therefore synthesised narratively, following the Synthesis Without Meta-analysis (SWiM) reporting guideline (Campbell et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Findings were therefore synthesised narratively, following the Synthesis Without Meta-analysis (SWiM) reporting guideline <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Campbell et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Studies were grouped according to the primary mental health condition the DMHI focused on.

Within each group, the direction of effect on the prespecified primary mental health outcome was used as the standardised metric, with effect estimates and confidence intervals reported where available.
Where studies reported multiple measures of the same mental health outcome, priority was given to the study's prespecified primary outcome.
Statistical significance was not used as the primary basis for determining DMHI effectiveness.
Variation in effects was considered descriptively in relation to study design, comparator, outcome measurement, follow-up and methodological quality.
Findings were tabulated by mental health target alongside these characteristics.

Formal GRADE assessment was not undertaken because the evidence base was dominated by small pilot studies, uncontrolled pre-post designs, heterogeneous interventions and outcome measures, and limited comparable between-group data.
Conclusions were interpreted considering the number and design of contributing studies, methodological and reporting quality, consistency of effects and precision where available.
Methodological and reporting quality was assessed using the Quality Assessment with Diverse Studies (QuADS; (Harrison et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Methodological and reporting quality was assessed using the Quality Assessment with Diverse Studies (QuADS; <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Harrison et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Given the heterogeneous study designs expected in the search yield, this tool allowed for meaningful comparisons across different study methodologies.
The QuADS includes 13 items, each scored on a 4-point (0 to 3) scale, with the highest possible overall score being 39.
Two sample items include "Appropriate sampling to address the stated research aim/s" and 'The method of analysis was appropriate to answer the research aim/s".
Two authors (XX and XX) collaboratively appraised 20% of the studies.
Then, they each independently appraised 60% of the studies to allow for interrater reliability, which allowed for 20% to be double rated and interrater reliability evaluated.
Interrater reliability (κ = 0.703, 95% CI [0.57, 0.84]) was adequate and met the a priori (κ ≥ 0.7) threshold for acceptability (McHugh, 2012).
text.formatted: Interrater reliability (κ = 0.703, 95% CI [0.57, 0.84]) was adequate and met the a priori (κ ≥ 0.7) threshold for acceptability <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(McHugh, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: The authorship team consists of two autistic researchers and one otherwise neurodivergent researcher who have experience in clinical and experimental psychology.
Their blend of lived and professional experiences guided the design, conduct, and reporting of this review.

Language use was informed by the team's lived experience and the preferences of the autistic and autism community; as such, identity-first language (e.g., "autistic people"; Kenny et al., 2016) is used.
text.formatted: Language use was informed by the team's lived experience and the preferences of the autistic and autism community; as such, identity-first language (e.g., "autistic people"; <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Kenny et al., 2016)</ref> is used.

text.text: The authors are at different stages of their research careers, and all aim to adopt neurodiversity-affirming, participatory research approaches in their work.
Overall, 33 reports were included in this review, reporting on 1,089 autistic participants (1,258 before attrition).
Tables 1 and 2 contain the main study and participant characteristics for all studies in aggregate.
text.formatted: Tables <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref> and <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref> contain the main study and participant characteristics for all studies in aggregate.

text.text: See Supplementary Materials A for the characteristics of each included study and their participants.
Fifteen studies were randomised controlled trials (RCTs; 45.45%), and one additional study included a comparison group.
The remaining 17 studies (51.52%) used uncontrolled single-group, case-series or case-study designs.
Studies were conducted in 9 countries, predominantly the United States (k = 15), United Kingdom (k = 8) and Australia (k = 3).
Only one study was conducted outside of Western countries with predominantly White, English-speaking populations.
Across the 31 studies that reported participant age, the mean age was 23.22 years (range 4-77 years).

Based on reported age ranges, 19 studies reported on autistic children or adolescents (age 6-17 years), 11 on autistic adults (18-77 years) and three reported on both adolescents and adults (one 13-24 years, one 16-74, and one 16-64).

Reporting of sex and gender was inconsistent: 20 studies reported gender only, two sex only, three both, and seven used male/female categories without specifying the construct and two provided no numerical breakdown.
Only six studies reported gender beyond binary categories, within which 2.9% of participants identified as having a non-binary gender.
Across the studies which reported gender (k = 20, n = 768), the percentage of men was 53.91%, the percentage of women was 37.89%, and the percentage of gender diverse participants was 6.90%.
In studies which reported sex (k = 5, n = 359) the percentage of males was 38.99% and the percentage of females was 60.72%.

In studies which did not clearly define if they were reporting sex or gender (k = 7, n = 196) the percentage of male/men participants was 70.41% and the percentage of female/women participants was 29.59%.
Participants with a co-occurring ID were explicitly excluded in 18 (54.54%) studies; ten of these reported specific exclusion criteria (e.g., IQ cutoffs) while eight did not (summarised in Table 2).
text.formatted: Participants with a co-occurring ID were explicitly excluded in 18 (54.54%) studies; ten of these reported specific exclusion criteria (e.g., IQ cutoffs) while eight did not (summarised in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref>).

text.text: Four studies included participants with an ID, totalling six participants.
This is equivalent to 7.79% of the total participants in those four studies or 0.48% of the participants across all studies.
No studies focused exclusively on participants with ID.

Socioeconomic status was reported in 16 studies, most commonly using parental education and/or income as a proxy, with a smaller number reporting participant education, maternal education, or area-level socioeconomic status.
Varied reporting practices precluded meaningful aggregation of the data, but samples tended to have high levels of income and education.
See Supplementary Materials A for a detailed summary of the participant socioeconomic characteristics reported in each study.
Ethnicity was reported to some extent in 26 studies.
Reporting practices varied widely but the average proportion of White participants was 76% (range 43-97%).
Overall, 29 different therapy programs were reported across the 33 included studies.
Tables 3 and 4 report aggregated intervention characteristics and outcomes.
text.formatted: Tables <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">3</ref> and <ref type="table" target="#tab_3">4</ref> report aggregated intervention characteristics and outcomes.

text.text: See Supplementary Materials C for the individual characteristics of each study.
The majority of DMHIs primarily targeted anxiety disorders (k = 23; 69.7%), including four that focused on specific phobias.
Other primary targets included (non-specific) "mental health" (k = 4), depression (k = 3), OCD (k = 2), trauma (k = 2), self-compassion (k = 1), and internalising symptoms (k = 1).
Most studies had a single primary DMHI target but measured multiple additional secondary outcomes.
Most DMHIs were based on cognitive behavioural therapy (k = 22; 66.6%).
Other DMHI frameworks included mindfulness (k = 6), compassion-focused approaches (k = 2), biofeedback (k = 1), and dialectical behavioural therapy (k = 1).
Autism-specific tailoring of DMHIs was reported in 18 studies (54.54%).
Tailoring included adaptations to DMHI content, language and visual presentation, session structure and delivery, and inclusion of autism-specific topics such as sensory experiences.
Some DMHIs also incorporated individual customisation or autistic input into intervention materials.
DMHIs were delivered through video calls (k = 14), mobile applications (k = 7), and websites/webpages (k = 4).
Less common approaches included virtual reality, self-guided modules, video games, email, SMS monitoring and biofeedback devices.
Clinicians or researchers were involved in 26 studies, with categories of involvement not mutually exclusive.
Involvement most often occurred through direct delivery (k = 14), a contactable therapist (k = 6) or therapist in the room while DMHI is being completed (k = 6).
Table 3 summarises reported methods of clinician or researcher involvement across interventions.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">3</ref> summarises reported methods of clinician or researcher involvement across interventions.

text.text: Nineteen studies evaluated DMHIs primarily targeting anxiety disorders other than specific phobias.
Eleven included a comparator, of which ten were RCTs and one was a non-randomised waitlist pilot.
Eight studies were uncontrolled or did not use their control group in the analysis.
Among the 11 studies with a comparator, four reported results favouring the DMHI on the primary anxiety outcome and three reported little or no difference between conditions.

Two did not provide sufficient information to determine the direction of effect; one could not complete the planned between-group analysis, and one active-comparator pilot reported pre-post improvement without evidence that either support format was superior.
Among studies without a usable comparator, anxiety generally decreased from pre-to post-intervention, although findings were mixed within some studies and across outcome measures.
Because these studies did not include between-group comparison, they provide weaker evidence of DMHI effects.
Four studies evaluated DMHIs targeting specific phobia or fear.
One was a randomised controlled feasibility trial, in which 4/16 participants in the intervention group versus 0/16 controls responded at two weeks.
Three uncontrolled studies reported pre-post findings that indicated positive response to the DMHI.
Whilst these findings are promising, they should be interpreted cautiously as the samples were small and there were limited data from control participants.
Three studies primarily targeted depression; one RCT and two uncontrolled case series.
The RCT reported results favouring the DMHI.
A case series showed reliable improvement in depression in one of six participants, with variable changes across participants and measures.

The other uncontrolled study reported reduced depressive symptoms on the PHQ-9 from baseline to outcome, but little change on another depression measure and no significant change in weekly PHQ-9 ratings.
Overall, findings provide preliminary support for some approaches, but evidence remains limited and varies by intervention, measure and assessment timing.
Two studies evaluated DMHIs that included OCD as a primary target.
Both used active-comparator designs involving different modes of therapist support.
OCD symptoms improved from pre-to postintervention, but there was no clear evidence that one digital delivery format was superior to the other.
Two uncontrolled studies evaluated telehealth-delivered trauma-focused interventions.
Both reported reductions in trauma-related distress or PTSD symptoms from pre-to post-intervention, with mixed findings for resilience or related outcomes.
These preliminary pre-post findings do not provide comparative evidence of efficacy.

Studies targeting broader mental health, self-compassion or internalising symptoms reported mixed but generally promising pre-post changes across depression, anxiety, wellbeing, emotion regulation and self-compassion outcomes.
Because these studies were largely uncontrolled or used outcomes beyond the prespecified primary target, findings are summarised descriptively rather than as comparative efficacy estimates.
Anxiety was the most frequently assessed outcome (k = 31), followed by depression (k = 12 studies).
PTSD-related outcomes were assessed in two studies, while OCD and general mental health were each assessed in one study.
Studies also assessed related outcomes, including stress, emotion regulation, wellbeing, self-compassion, mindfulness, quality of life, and internalising and externalising difficulties.
Measurement was highly heterogeneous, with 29 anxiety measures and 10 depression measures, plus additional measures of PTSD, OCD and other mental health-related outcomes.
Table 4 lists the most frequently used measures, and all measures are outlined in Supplementary Materials D.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_3">4</ref> lists the most frequently used measures, and all measures are outlined in Supplementary Materials D.

text.text: Consideration of measurement appropriateness for autistic people was limited.
Six studies used measures developed or adapted for autistic people, five studies cited autism-specific psychometric evidence, and six referred to previous use in autistic samples.
Sixteen studies (48.48%) provided no autism-specific justification for the measures used.
Completion rates were reported in 23 studies, totalling 1,011 participants with attrition data.
In total, 169 autistic participants were lost to attrition and 842 completed the studies, corresponding to an overall completion rate of 83.28% and an attrition rate of 16.72%.
Fifteen studies reported engagement or satisfaction, most commonly using the Client Satisfaction Questionnaire (n = 5).
Six studies used unvalidated satisfaction or engagement measures such as bespoke questionnaires or participation metrics.
Two studies used other validated measures of telehealth or mobile-app satisfaction.
The mean QuADS score was 29.79 (SD = 3.93) with a range of 22 to 36 (maximum possible 39).

Highest scores were observed for reporting research aims (M = 2.87, SD = 0.33), appropriateness of data collection tools (M = 2.81, SD = 0.39) and rationale for outcome selection (M = 2.76, SD = 0.67).
Lower scores were related to interest holder involvement (M = 0.7, SD = 1.10), justification of analytic methods (M = 1.45, SD = 1.18), and consideration of sample size (M = 1.85, SD = 0.97).
Community involvement was limited; five (15.2%) studies reported any community involvement in the study design and four (12.12%) in the DMHI design.
This includes two studies which had community involvement in both study and DMHI design.
See Table 5, which summarises author-described community involvement using the participatory ladder outlined by den Houting et al. (2021).
text.formatted: See Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_4">5</ref>, which summarises author-described community involvement using the participatory ladder outlined by den <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Houting et al. (2021)</ref>.

text.text: To our knowledge, this is the first systematic review of studies evaluating DMHIs for autistic people.
Findings suggest that the evidence relating to DMHIs is in the early stages; over half of the studies are pilots, feasibility studies, case series or uncontrolled studies.

The range of DMHIs explored is also in its infancy; the clear focus of the research on DMHIs for autistic people has been on anxiety (69.7%) and amongst those with control comparisons, the findings have been mixed.
Although there have only been two controlled studies exploring DMHIs for depression in autistic people, both suggested positive effects of the DMHI, indicating potential for this area.
However, sample descriptions were often limited, but reported demographics suggest a lack of diversity.
All but one of the studies was conducted in a Western context and the mean proportion of White participants was 76%.

Finally, the review identified some clear directions for future research, including DMHIs co-designed with autistic input using frameworks outside of CBT and those evaluated using measures designed and validated for autistic people.
Across the studies included in this review, the clinical targets of DMHIs evaluated for autistic people were concentrated within a relatively narrow range of conditions.
Anxiety was the most common target, which is understandable given that it is often described as the mental health condition with the highest prevalence among autistic people (Micai et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Anxiety was the most common target, which is understandable given that it is often described as the mental health condition with the highest prevalence among autistic people <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Micai et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: This focus on anxiety, although consistent with the focus of DMHIs in the broader digital mental health literature (Crocamo et al., 2025), has left other mental health conditions relatively unexplored.
text.formatted: This focus on anxiety, although consistent with the focus of DMHIs in the broader digital mental health literature <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Crocamo et al., 2025)</ref>, has left other mental health conditions relatively unexplored.

text.text: This review showed one study suggesting preliminary promising evidence for DMHIs targeting depression, and the broader DMHI literature for non-autistic people suggests potential for DMHI for bipolar and psychotic disorders (Crocamo et al., 2025).
text.formatted: This review showed one study suggesting preliminary promising evidence for DMHIs targeting depression, and the broader DMHI literature for non-autistic people suggests potential for DMHI for bipolar and psychotic disorders <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Crocamo et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Given that autistic people may experience higher rates of, and poorer outcomes associated with, these conditions (Underwood et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2021), developing and evaluating autism-focused DMHIs beyond anxiety (that consider clinical safety, crisis pathways and the preferences of autistic people) could be an important research pathway.
text.formatted: Given that autistic people may experience higher rates of, and poorer outcomes associated with, these conditions <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Underwood et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Zheng et al., 2021)</ref>, developing and evaluating autism-focused DMHIs beyond anxiety (that consider clinical safety, crisis pathways and the preferences of autistic people) could be an important research pathway.

text.text: Although a large proportion of the DMHIs focused on anxiety, limitations in study quality and certainty of the available evidence mean that the effectiveness of DMHIs for anxiety in autistic people remains unclear.

Findings cannot yet establish whether anxiety-focused DMHIs are effective for autistic people as comparative results were mixed, many studies were small pilot or feasibility studies, outcome measures varied substantially, and several studies were uncontrolled.

Larger, adequately powered randomised controlled trials with appropriate comparators, autism-informed outcome measures, longer follow-up and transparent reporting of attrition and adverse effects are therefore needed.
Therapeutic diversity of the DMHIs was limited, with the vast majority of DMHIs evaluated for autistic people being based on a CBT framework.
This reflects the broader DMHI literature, in which CBT and third-wave CBT approaches are prominent (Crocamo et al., 2025).
text.formatted: This reflects the broader DMHI literature, in which CBT and third-wave CBT approaches are prominent <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Crocamo et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: However, a recent meta-analysis of digitally delivered third-wave therapies for depression and anxiety in nonautistic populations reported small-to-moderate reductions in anxiety and depression, although the anxiety findings were heterogeneous (Ip et al., 2026).
text.formatted: However, a recent meta-analysis of digitally delivered third-wave therapies for depression and anxiety in nonautistic populations reported small-to-moderate reductions in anxiety and depression, although the anxiety findings were heterogeneous <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Ip et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: This suggests that DMHIs may have the potential to deliver a range of therapeutic approaches.

Although (adapted) CBT has demonstrated efficacy for some autistic people (Roberts & Rankin, 2025), qualitative research indicates mixed views about its acceptability, fit and accessibility, especially when unadapted (Di Marco et al., 2025; Roisenberg et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Although (adapted) CBT has demonstrated efficacy for some autistic people <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Roberts & Rankin, 2025)</ref>, qualitative research indicates mixed views about its acceptability, fit and accessibility, especially when unadapted <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Di Marco et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Roisenberg et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Future DMHI research should broaden the adaptations made to CBT along with broadening the range of therapeutic approaches available to allow autistic people a choice of approaches and forms of support that align with their needs, availability and preferences.
The need for accessible and effective autism-specific mental health supports is clear (Roche et al., 2021); <anonymised for review>).
text.formatted: The need for accessible and effective autism-specific mental health supports is clear <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Roche et al., 2021)</ref>; <anonymised for review>).

text.text: Although DMHIs may address some of the barriers autistic people face in accessing mental health supports, digital delivery alone does not guarantee accessibility or effectiveness.
Autism-informed adaptation of mental health supports developed for non-autistic people may improve their effectiveness for autistic people (Linden et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Autism-informed adaptation of mental health supports developed for non-autistic people may improve their effectiveness for autistic people <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Linden et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Conversely, inappropriate supports can have harmful effects; repeatedly seeking and not receiving appropriate support can cause growing feelings of hopelessness, isolation, and despair in autistic people and their caregivers, which in turn can exacerbate mental health difficulties (including suicidality), cause or contribute to burnout, and lead to disengagement from health-care services (Brede et al., 2022; Wechsler et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Conversely, inappropriate supports can have harmful effects; repeatedly seeking and not receiving appropriate support can cause growing feelings of hopelessness, isolation, and despair in autistic people and their caregivers, which in turn can exacerbate mental health difficulties (including suicidality), cause or contribute to burnout, and lead to disengagement from health-care services <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Brede et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Wechsler et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Against this background, it is concerning that only about half of the studies in this review (that focuses on papers reporting outcomes of DMHIs) reported tailoring or adapting the DMHI for autistic people.
Adaptations that were undertaken were predominantly minor changes to intervention content, language, visual presentation, session structure or delivery.
Adaptations were not consistently based on input from autistic people themselves.
In fact, only four studies reported community involvement in DMHI design, and only half of these were described as consultation or engagement rather than co-production.
Only five studies reported community involvement in the broader study design, such as outcome measures or processes.

Co-design and participatory approaches can help ensure that interventions reflect autistic people's priorities, communication styles and lived experiences, and may improve engagement with supports (<anonymised for review>; (Crocker et al., 2018) and the translation of research into practice (Fletcher-Watson et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Co-design and participatory approaches can help ensure that interventions reflect autistic people's priorities, communication styles and lived experiences, and may improve engagement with supports (<anonymised for review>; <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Crocker et al., 2018)</ref> and the translation of research into practice <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Fletcher-Watson et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Future research should therefore move beyond adapting existing interventions for autistic people and work alongside autistic people to co-produce the interventions, select meaningful outcomes and interpret the findings.
In doing so, the aim should not be to simply make DMHI available but to develop DMHIs that autistic people recognise as safe, accessible, acceptable and useful.
The included samples were geographically narrow.

All but one study was conducted in Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich, Democratic (WEIRD; (Rad et al., 2018) countries and the participants in the only study conducted in a non-Western country only make up 2.5% of total participants.
text.formatted: All but one study was conducted in Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich, Democratic (WEIRD; <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Rad et al., 2018)</ref> countries and the participants in the only study conducted in a non-Western country only make up 2.5% of total participants.

text.text: This dominance of WEIRD samples is similar to other areas of autism (Smart et al., 2026; White et al., 2025), and DMHI research (Croke et al., 2026; Fowler et al., 2023).

text.text: However, it is entirely unrepresentative of the global population distribution where 88% of the population reside in non-WEIRD countries (Henrich et al., 2010).
text.formatted: However, it is entirely unrepresentative of the global population distribution where 88% of the population reside in non-WEIRD countries <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Henrich et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Many non-WEIRD countries have higher levels of unmet need for mental health services (Patel et al., 2025) and DMHIs could be one potential way to address this challenge (Naslund et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Many non-WEIRD countries have higher levels of unmet need for mental health services <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Patel et al., 2025)</ref> and DMHIs could be one potential way to address this challenge <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Naslund et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Research developing DMHIs for autistic people in underrepresented countries and communities and evaluating their uptake and effectiveness is therefore needed.
Autistic people with co-occurring ID were also substantially underrepresented in the studies reviewed.

Most studies excluded or did not report including participants with ID, despite estimates suggesting that a substantial minority of autistic people have a co-occurring ID (Russell et al., 2019; Salkić et al., 2026).

text.text: Future studies should actively include autistic people with intellectual disability and report the adaptations required to support their participation.
As with any review, the results must be considered alongside the limitations.
The review adhered to PRISMA systematic review processes and SWiM reporting approaches.
However, because of limitations in the evidence-base, it was not possible to undertake a meta-analysis with the evidence available at the current time.

As research progresses, using a meta-analysis will allow for statistical synthesis of findings as well as explorations of moderators of effectiveness, which can in turn assist with tailoring of approaches into the future.

An important addition of a future metaanalysis would be an evaluation of publication bias, as publishing studies with non-significant effects can be more challenging than those reporting significant effects.
The review did not place any language restrictions on articles, but all search terms were in English so for articles to be found, they had to include English titles, keywords or abstracts.

It may also be that some studies delivered mental health supports in digital formats but only describe this in their method; these would not have been identified using the search terms included in this review.
This review found that research on DMHIs for autistic people is promising but remains at an early stage.

The evidence is concentrated on anxiety and CBT-based interventions, but findings from comparative studies are mixed and the predominance of small, pilot and uncontrolled studies prevents firm conclusions about efficacy.
The current evidence base also represents only a narrow proportion of autistic people, with limited inclusion of people with intellectual disability and participants from non-Western settings.
Future progress requires more than increasing the number of DMHIs or studies on DMHIs.
Studies should be adequately powered, use outcome measures that are meaningful and appropriate for autistic people, include longer-term follow-up and report harms and attrition transparently.
Autistic people should be involved throughout the research process, including in defining priorities, co-producing interventions and selecting outcomes.
Expanding both the conditions targeted and the therapeutic approaches evaluated is also essential.
This would ensure that DMHIs are not simply made available, but they are accessible, acceptable and clinically useful supports for autistic people around the world.
